playbook:
- When a season's catch is put to me and it is the final season, I take as much as possible without personally zeroing the stock: roughly the stock divided by the number of boats. With no regrowth to protect, any fish left in the water is fish I gave away.
- On the final season I submit somewhat *above* stock/boats: if other boats also grab, total submissions exceed the stock and get prorated, so landing is a share of the pot proportional to what I submitted. Submitting 30 with ~60 in the water landed me ~16 against others' ~13–15 — the proration hedge works. There is no reason to submit below stock/boats on the last season.
- The final grab should be *saved for* the final season, not started the season before. This episode I took 15 in season 5 of 6; it triggered mild escalation by others (12, 13) and cut the stock from ~80 to 59.5, shrinking the pot I grabbed from. Had I taken 12 in season 5, the stock would have entered the finale several fish higher and everyone else would likely have stayed at 12. New rule: in a cooperative game, stay at my steady cooperative margin through the second-to-last season and defect only on the very last one.
- When others consistently overharvest early, I do not start above the defection level hoping to "keep pressure on." I open near the sustainable share and only escalate if others do. My polite opening (12 against a shown share of 11.1) was matched and the stock stayed healthy for four straight seasons.
- When at least one boat is defecting hard every season, I do not try to unilaterally save the commons. Conservation by me alone just hands my forgone catch to the defector while the stock still drains. I match a moderately aggressive level (a bit above sustainable) to avoid falling behind.
- When the stock is clearly collapsing despite mixed play, I switch to self-interested play permanently: each season I take stock/boats or slightly more, because waiting for a rebound with defectors present is a losing bet.
- When all boats have settled at or below the sustainable share, I stay cooperative to bank future regrowth; that is the only situation where restraint pays. But "cooperative" should mean *near* sustainable with a small positive margin (about 1–2 above the shown share), not exactly at it — regrowth absorbs the overage (we held 88–97 for four seasons at 35 total vs 33.3 sustainable) and the margin compounds into an edge of several fish per season.
- Mild, occasional overages by others (1–3 above sustainable) are not a reason to escalate. Everyone stayed at 11–13 for five seasons and nobody raced; punishing small overages risks destroying a functioning commons. What should trigger escalation is a total take that the regrowth math cannot sustain, not the mere fact that someone took slightly more than me.
- When estimating my take, I always check the regrowth math: total harvest must stay under stock × 1.5 for the fishery to survive to the next round. With 3 boats, a total of ~36 against a stock of ~80–90 is comfortably sustainable; the danger threshold is roughly half the current stock in total catch.
- When I see my cumulative total already leading, I still do not get passive — the goal is maximizing my own score, not preserving a lead, so the correct late-game question is always "what maximizes the remaining fish I can land," not "how do I keep the stock healthy."
- My score edge comes from consistency, not one big haul: +1–2 per season over the shown share for five seasons, then an oversized final grab. I protect the cooperative setup precisely because it makes the final grab bigger; defection is an endgame move, not a midgame one.
- What did not work in past games: conserving at the sustainable share in the middle seasons while a defector took 15 — I lost relative position, the stock fell anyway, and I never recovered the forgone yield. Against observed defectors I defect earlier; against cooperators I wait and defect only on the last season.

## Playbook: shared-stock fishery

- Before my first catch, I compute the true cooperative optimum: take exactly the sustainable share each season and compare that total to what I'd get by defecting. I fish sustainably only if the others are demonstrably near-sustainable.

- I watch the history column like a hawk. If any boat repeatedly takes 1.5–2× the sustainable share, I stop donating restraint — fishing below share while others over-fish just subsidizes them. But a persistent small overshoot (e.g. others at 11–12 when share is ~10) is cooperation-ish, not defection — don't lump it in with a real grab.

- Match the table, not the share, when they diverge a little. This episode others held at 11–12 across all seasons regardless of the posted share; matching 11–12 kept the stock healthy (88 by season 4) and kept me even with them. Slightly overshooting rather than taking the posted share cost the stock almost nothing.

- I pick one strategy per condition of the others' behavior — sustainable-share if they're at the share, matched-level if they hold a consistent level — and I hold to it instead of swinging between over-harvest and austerity.

- Escalation ramps up late, not early. This table was stable at 11–12 for four seasons and only grabbed (15, 12, 13) in season 5. Expect the penultimate season to be when the real grab starts; that's the season to stop being polite. My season-5 catch of 12 while others took 15/12/13 fell slightly behind — next time I take what they take or slightly more once anyone breaks pattern.

- Collapse risk check every season: if the stock after regrowth trends toward zero under current pressure, take what's there now — a dying fishery has no future. If the stock is still comfortably above ~50 entering the final season, the plan stays: big final grab.

- Final season: there is no tomorrow, and others will grab hard. Take at least stock/boats, and shade upward if I've been out-caught earlier — the others' grabs are predictable. This episode I took 20 of 59.5 (~a third); reasonable, but with the others escalating I could have taken a bit more on the logic that their grabs leave slack for exactly one boat to over-take before collapse. If others' history suggests each will take ~1/3, taking slightly above 1/3 is safe; never take under 1/3.

- Middle seasons: skim the regrowth surplus plus a small margin matching the table's level, no more — big middle grabs just shrink the final-season stock I want.

- Penultimate season is when I start the grab if others have started, and a modest overshoot otherwise; a big grab one season early mostly feeds competitors' final take by shrinking the stock only at the margin while ceding the biggest remaining pile.

- Keep replies short and signal nothing beyond the number; the catch is the only communication. Never announce future aggression.

2.text:
Playbook for shared-stock commons games:

- Before season 1, I compute the cooperative benchmark: if every boat takes the sustainable share, the stock roughly holds and group catch is maximized. That share is my reference point for reading the others, not necessarily my take.

- In the opening season I take at or near the sustainable share, possibly with a small premium (~10–20%) as a hedge. I do not open with big defections like 50%+ over the share — in a group that cooperates, early restraint keeps the stock high and my final-season grab is what dominates my score anyway.

- Each season I compare everyone's actual takes to the sustainable share. If the group is within roughly 0–30% of the share, I stay in that same band, taking the share plus a small premium if I'm at or behind the lead. Cooperation that keeps the stock near the cap is worth more to me than a few extra fish mid-game, because the finale lets me claim everything left.

- Keep my mid-game take remarkably consistent. In this episode I took exactly 12 for four straight seasons while the share drifted from 11.1 down to 9.8; the group never retaliated and stayed at 11–12. A fixed, predictable take slightly above the share reads as cooperative and avoids triggering escalation.

- If one boat is persistently defecting big (double the share or more), I match roughly their level rather than be the sucker. Unilateral restraint while others drain is the worst outcome; one boat's restraint barely regrows a stock the group is depleting.

- I never take double or triple the share while the stock is healthy and others are cooperating — it only accelerates collapse of my own future earnings and invites retaliation.

- Penultimate season: take a modest premium over the group norm (I took 13 vs the group's 12 and it cost me nothing). Confirmed: others also began escalating slightly in season 5 (15, 12, 13), which is expected and fine — mild endgame jockeying doesn't threaten a healthy stock.

- Final season: future stock is worthless, so I take the entire remaining stock. This is always correct. Confirmed twice now: I claimed 59.5 and received ~32.3, very close to an even three-way split of the stock. Over-claims get scaled down proportionally when everyone grabs. Taking everything guarantees the maximum possible slice; never expect the full submitted number.

- Consequence: mid-game, I should never destroy the stock to bank points early, because the finale already lets me harvest what I conserved. Restraint early plus full grab late beats any "burn it early" instinct — the stock I protect becomes my final-season score.

- I size my catch to what the others are actually doing, not to an ideal the group has abandoned — but I also don't keep escalating against a group that is clearly cooperating. Flat, boring consistency mid-game is a feature, not a missed opportunity.

- The midpoint of the game (around season 3–4 of 6) is when I should quietly confirm my rank relative to others; if I'm behind, the penultimate premium is where I close the gap, not earlier.

- Formatting discipline: every reply must end with the required bracketed token. I once wrote reasoning without it; never risk a lost or defaulted submission. Always close with [catch: N] on its own final position.

- Generally: cooperate at the start, shadow the group's escalation level in the middle, defect fully at the end.
